theses.one_liner: T-Minus is the AI that calls your phone at your freeze-prone moments and talks your body through the first two minutes — because a frozen person can't open an app, but almost anyone can answer a ringing phone.
theses.target_user: Maya, 34, product-marketing manager, diagnosed at 31 — squarely in the surge cohort (new ADHD diagnoses among women 23-49 nearly doubled 2020-2022, per Epic Research). Remote three days a week, medicated during work hours but not evenings. Her three daily freezes: 7:15am bed-to-shower paralysis, the 10:00am 'open the document' start, and the 8:30pm kitchen reset after meds wear off. She already owns the graveyard: Goblin Tools (loved, but 'it hands me a list'), Finch (abandoned week 3), Focusmate (used twice, never booked a third session because booking was itself a task). She does not need another list, another streak, or another human stranger on video. She needs the start command to come from outside her own head.
winning_problem: Cluster 1: Task Initiation Paralysis ("I know exactly what to do and cannot start") — specifically the slice the skeptic verdict left open: spontaneous, in-the-moment freeze rescue with no self-initiation required
Cluster 2: Every Coping Tool Stops Working — attacked structurally as a design requirement, not a feature
Secondary adjacency (v2): Cluster 6 Waiting Mode — the same trusted external time-guardian primitive extends to guarding an afternoon appointment
theses.product_concept:
T-Minus inverts the direction of every initiation tool on the market. Dubbii, Focusmate, Flow Club, Goblin Tools, and every routine app share one fatal architecture: the frozen user must reach for the tool. But the freeze IS the inability to reach. As the research puts it, every existing fix "requires the frozen person to self-initiate the fix with the exact faculty that is offline." T-Minus removes the reach: at launch windows you contracted with your past (unfrozen) self, your phone rings — a real PSTN call from a saved contact — and a warm, adaptive AI voice runs a launch sequence: "Don't get up yet. Just sit up and put both feet on the floor. Tell me when they're down." It stays on the line through the first physical action — feet on floor, water running, document open — then deliberately hangs up. It is not a coach, not a therapist, not a planner. It is a two-to-five-minute bridge from list-item to body-in-motion.

A day with it: the night before, a 90-second call ("Tomorrow: out of bed by 7:40, start the deck at 10. Anything else? No? Sleep well."). At 7:40 the phone rings on the nightstand — answering is the entire ask; the agent negotiates her vertical and into the shower, and hangs up when she says the water is on. At 10:02 it calls again: "Deck open? I'll wait... okay, type the title slide while I'm here." At 9pm, unscheduled couch lock hits — the Black Hole Chair. She taps the Launch button on her lock screen (one tap, zero navigation, no chat UI) and her phone rings back within seconds: "Kitchen night. We're just carrying one plate to the sink. Take me with you."

There is no to-do list in T-Minus. No streaks, no overdue counters, no red badges. Missed calls are never mentioned. The only number that exists anywhere is a lifetime count of starts. And crucially, there is no app you must remember to open: you can forget T-Minus exists and it still calls you tomorrow. That single property is why this product's week 6 looks different from the graveyard's.

The thesis respects the skeptic's downgrade honestly. The verdict said initiation is not an empty field — Dubbii has 500k+ users, Focusmate externalizes starts for scheduled work — and named the genuinely unclaimed slice: "spontaneous, in-the-moment freeze rescue with no self-initiation required." T-Minus is purpose-built for exactly that slice, plus the scheduled freezes, with the trigger living outside the user in both cases. We position against Dubbii directly: their videos are static, identical on every play (habituation fuel), and require the frozen person to open an app, choose a video, and press play. Our call arrives, is different every time, and talks back.
theses.core_loop: 1. EVENING CONTRACT (90 seconds, voice): T-Minus calls at a chosen wind-down time. User names tomorrow's 1-3 launch windows — not tasks, just moments the body needs to start moving ("out of bed 7:40", "start the report at 10"). No forms, ever. 2. THE CALL: at each window the phone rings (real call, saved contact, chosen ringtone). Answering is the only required act. 3. LAUNCH SEQUENCE: the agent runs a countdown protocol — second-person, imperative, micro-physical steps ("speaker on, walk to the bathroom, tell me when the water's running") — adapting live to resistance ("I can't" → "Okay. Just sit up. That's the whole job."). It stays on the line through the first physical action, confirms ignition, and hangs up within 5 minutes by design. 4. RESCUE PATH (unscheduled freezes): one tap on a lock-screen Launch button triggers a callback in seconds — for couch lock, shower avoidance, the 9pm kitchen. One tap is the entire self-initiation budget we ask of a frozen person; everything after arrives inbound. 5. MISS PROTOCOL (deterministic, promised in advance): unanswered call → one retry after 10 minutes → one no-guilt SMS ("Here when you want me. Reply GO for a call.") → silence. Never a third attempt, never a badge, never a mention of the miss on the next call. 6. WEEKLY TUNE (voice, 3 minutes): the agent reports answer-rate patterns and proposes one change — shift a window, swap voice, switch a window to SMS-first — and asks consent. The system visibly notices when it stops working and changes itself, instead of making the user confess failure.
theses.why_ai_is_essential: Three load-bearing jobs are impossible without LLMs. (1) NEGOTIATION: getting a frozen human into motion is a live, adaptive conversation — the agent must respond to "I can't," "five more minutes," "I don't know where to start," and shrink the ask in real time. A robocall or recorded video cannot do this; that category is called an alarm, and alarms are precisely what ADHD brains habituate through (the research's notification-blindness thread). (2) INFINITE SCRIPT VARIABILITY: habituation feeds on sameness. Every T-Minus call has a generated, never-repeated opening and phrasing, tuned to time of day, task, and what worked in past transcripts. Static content — Dubbii's videos, a fixed alarm tone — is structurally identical on play 40 as on play 1. (3) PER-PERSON LEARNING: transcripts reveal which framings move this specific user (humor vs drill-sergeant vs gentle; body-first vs environment-first) and feed the weekly self-tuning. Pre-LLM, the only product delivering adaptive spoken launch support was a human — an ADHD coach at $100+/hour or a patient partner, neither available at 7:15am daily nor at 9pm on the couch. Real-time voice models priced at cents per minute are what makes a daily, personal, conversational starter economically possible for $12/month. Without AI, T-Minus degrades into a scheduled robocall: it would habituate in weeks and could not negotiate — the product literally does not exist.
non_ai_features: The Launch Button: a lock-screen widget / iOS Shortcut that triggers a callback. Deterministic, zero AI, zero latency, zero decisions — at the freeze moment, reliability beats intelligence, and one tap is the maximum self-initiation a frozen person can be asked for.

The Miss Protocol: hard-coded escalation ladder (one retry after 10 min, one SMS, then silence). Promised in onboarding and never varied — predictability is how we rebuild the trust in external signals that snoozed alarms destroyed.
Quiet hours and do-not-call windows: user-set, absolute, and the AI can never override or 'decide' to call anyway. Trust primitive, not a model output.

Auto-pause billing: if no call is answered and no button tapped for 21 days, the subscription pauses itself and billing stops — a dumb cron job, deliberately outside AI control, that is the anti-ADHD-tax core of the business model.
The Starts counter: a plain lifetime tally of launches. No streaks, no AI judgment, no 'insights.' Arithmetic only, because any scoring of the user is shame surface area.
In-call task timers (shower timer, 10-minute kitchen reset): simple visual/audio countdowns with no AI, running after the agent hangs up.
theses.anti_habituation_design: Cluster 2 says the median tool loses 70% of users within 100 days (JMIR 2024) and ADHD app death is 'three days of enthusiasm, then forget it exists' (Lunatask). T-Minus survives week 6 through five concrete mechanics. (1) STRUCTURAL IMMUNITY TO FORGETTING: the dominant abandonment mode is forgetting to open the app. T-Minus has no daily app-open; the product arrives inbound. You can forget it exists and it still calls tomorrow — abandonment requires an active act (blocking the number or replying STOP), which we detect instantly. (2) VARIABILITY AS ANTI-HABITUATION: alarm habituation is driven by identical stimuli; every call differs in opening line, phrasing, and tactic (generated per-call), and a ringing phone from a known contact carries social answer-reflex weight that a notification banner lost years ago. This is our riskiest bet and we instrument it directly. (3) DUOLINGO-STYLE IGNORE DETECTION: we adopt the published sleeping-bandit pattern (Yancey & Settles, KDD 2020) as the template the skeptic verdict itself pointed to — answer rate, pickup latency, and launch confirmation are tracked per window; five consecutive misses on a window triggers self-modification ('These morning calls aren't landing. Want texts instead, or a different time, or a week off?') including graceful self-silencing with a standing re-entry path. The tool notices it is being ignored and changes itself, which the verdict confirmed no task/reminder product does. (4) ZERO SHAME SURFACE: no streaks to break, no overdue cascade (the 87-red-tasks death spiral), no history of misses visible anywhere, agent never references a failed launch. Amnesty is not a reset button — it is the absence of anything to reset. (5) EFFORT ASYMMETRY: total system maintenance is one 90-second evening call and one 3-minute weekly call, both inbound and voice-only. There is no elaborate setup to collapse under its own executive-function cost. Week 6 checkpoint in metrics: we measure answered-call rate and launch-confirmation rate at weeks 2/6/10 as the primary KPI — not DAU — and the bandit's job is to keep answered-rate flat where every competitor's open-rate curve cliffs.

competitors.name: Dubbii (body-doubling app by ADHD Love, 500k+ users)
competitors.gap: Static pre-recorded follow-along videos that are identical on every play (habituation fuel), and the frozen user must self-initiate: open the app, browse, choose a video, press play — the exact faculty that is offline. No proactive trigger, no live adaptation, no ignore-detection.

competitors.name: Focusmate
competitors.gap: Externalizes the start only for tasks scheduled in advance with a human stranger on video; booking a session is itself an initiation task, sessions are 25-75 min desk-work shaped, and it is useless for the 7:15am bed freeze or 9pm couch lock. Social overhead makes it aversive for the RSD-prone.

competitors.name: Flow Club
competitors.gap: $29/mo group work sessions; same self-initiation and scheduling burden, oriented at knowledge-work blocks, not showers, kitchens, or getting out of bed — where the research shows the freeze actually lives.

competitors.name: Goblin Tools (Magic ToDo)
competitors.gap: Owns task breakdown and is beloved — but stops at the list. Breakdown was never Maya's problem; the bridge from item #1 to body-in-motion is out of scope for Goblin, which makes it our ideal upstream neighbor, not a rival.

competitors.name: Mutra
competitors.gap: $7/mo peer task exchange for initiation; depends on posting tasks (self-initiation) and on human reciprocity and availability — no guarantee anyone shows up at your freeze moment, and asynchronous peers can't run a live launch sequence.

competitors.name: Finch / Routinery / Tiimo (routine + habit apps)
competitors.gap: All require remembering to open an app, all signal via notifications that habituate to invisibility, and none has in-the-moment rescue. Finch solved shame (non-punitive streaks) but not initiation — you can love your bird and still not get off the couch.

theses.business_model: $12/month or $96/year, flat, everything included — priced between Focusmate (~$8-12) and Flow Club ($29) with COGS of roughly 10-15 voice-minutes/day at cents per minute. The model is engineered against the ADHD tax the research documents (subscription flows that monetize forgetfulness; Monzo found ADHD money-management costs average ~£1,600/yr): (1) AUTO-PAUSE — 21 days with no answered call and no button tap pauses billing automatically and sends one notice; we structurally cannot earn zombie-subscription revenue, which converts Cluster 2's billing critique into our trust moat and marketing headline ('the subscription that cancels itself'). (2) Cancellation is replying STOP to a text — no flows, no retention screens. (3) No free-trial-to-annual-charge trap; trial ends in a pause, not a charge. (4) Monthly is the default at signup; annual is opt-in only, never pre-selected. The bet: in a market where the customer has been burned by every tool and billed for the corpse, provable billing integrity is acquisition fuel — this audience screenshots and shares it. Path to margin: voice costs fall quarterly; annual mix and a later partner/household tier ($18) lift ARPU without dark patterns.
theses.month_one_scope: SHIPS IN 30 DAYS (deliberately app-store-free): outbound PSTN calling agent (Twilio + a realtime voice LLM) with launch-sequence prompting for the five canonical freezes from the research — bed, shower, work-start, kitchen/tidy, leaving the house; 5-minute voice onboarding call; up to 3 daily launch windows; evening contract call; one-tap rescue via iOS Shortcut/lock-screen widget that requests a callback (plus 'call the contact yourself' as fallback); deterministic miss protocol (1 retry + 1 SMS + silence); rule-based adaptation v0 (5 misses on a window → offer change/pause via SMS); weekly starts-count SMS; auto-pause billing; Stripe + STOP-to-cancel. No native app required for MVP — a web onboarding page and a phone number is the whole product, which is why one founder plus one engineer can ship it this month. LATER (months 2-6): native iOS/Android app with widgets and Android quick-tile; bandit-based per-user script optimization on transcript outcomes; calendar-connected freeze-risk inference (call before the event Maya always freezes ahead of); silent co-presence mode (agent stays on the line quietly — body doubling without conversation); partner mode; Waiting-Mode Guardian (Cluster 6 expansion: 'I will call you at 3:10, hyperfocus freely until then'); voice persona marketplace.
riskiest_assumptions: People will answer repeated calls from an AI. The answer-reflex to a ringing phone may itself habituate, and some ADHD adults have phone aversion (Cluster 5's RSD/communication dread cuts against us). Mitigations: saved contact + chosen ringtone, SMS-first mode per window, and answered-rate as our week-2 kill metric. This is the assumption we test first, with 20 hand-recruited users, before writing much code.

Conversational voice guidance actually moves bodies better than static content. Body-doubling efficacy evidence is 'mixed' per the arxiv VR study cited in the skeptic verdict; we assume live negotiation outperforms Dubbii's videos but have no proof until we measure launch-confirmation rates.

A frozen person can execute even one tap. The verdict's own logic (the fix requires the offline faculty) applies to our rescue button; if in-the-moment taps don't happen, the scheduled inbound path must carry the product alone — which narrows us to predictable freezes.

Carrier spam filtering and iOS telephony constraints don't strangle deliverability — Twilio numbers can get flagged; mitigations are registered branded calling and VoIP-push fallback, but this is real operational risk for a calls-are-the-product company.
Unit economics hold if heavy users take 3 calls/day at 5 minutes each; voice-model pricing trends favor us but a $12 price point has thin margin at launch.

Willingness to pay from a burned-by-47-apps audience: trust deficit is severe (that's the point of Cluster 2), and our auto-pause billing deliberately sacrifices revenue to earn it — the model only works if integrity actually converts to word-of-mouth acquisition.

evidence_citations.claim: The freeze state is fully self-aware and volitional-but-blocked: 'I want to do the work. I know what I need to do... It feels like pushing magnets.'
Couch lock is real, named, and hours-long: 'The Black Hole Chair... Getting back out of that chair can feel like escaping the event horizon' (quote reconfirmed verbatim by skeptic).
The task itself is fine once started — initiation is the entire problem: 'once you're in the shower, it's usually fine. Sometimes it's great' (reconfirmed).
The freeze spans bed, scrolling, and hyperfixation exits: 'unable to get out of bed and start the day, stop scrolling and get off the toilet' (reconfirmed).
Median 70% of users abandon health apps within 100 days (n=525,824) — the cliff every tool in this market dies on and our KPI frame is built against.
The ADHD app death pattern is forgetting the app exists — which an inbound-call product structurally sidesteps: 'use it enthusiastically for three days, and then forget it exists.'
Overdue-count shame kills retention ('87 overdue tasks... opening the app triggers shame') — why T-Minus has no task list and no miss history (vendor-authored source, used directionally).
Users explicitly beg for amnesty mechanics: a Tody review requests 'a button to reset all tasks... without a cascade of overdue tasks hanging over you.'
Ignore-detecting, self-silencing, adaptive notification systems are proven at scale (Duolingo sleeping-bandit, KDD 2020) but absent from task/reminder tools — our adaptation template.
Primary competitor Dubbii (500k+ users) validates demand for guided task-starting but is static video requiring self-initiated app-opening.
Body doubling shows promise (85% of 220 neurodivergent participants reported task-completion improvement in one 2024 study) but scheduled-peer models carry booking overhead.
Market timing: 15.5M US adults with current ADHD diagnosis (CDC), and new diagnoses among women 23-49 nearly doubled 2020-2022 (Epic Research) — our beachhead persona cohort.
ADHD money-management costs average ~£1,600/yr (Monzo/YouGov) — context for why anti-ADHD-tax billing (auto-pause, STOP-to-cancel) is both ethical and a differentiator.

theses.why_i_win: Other teams will pick richer-sounding clusters and inherit their poison pills. The ADHD-tax team (Cluster 4) needs bank integrations, biller phone calls, and financial-data trust — not shippable by a small team in 30 days, and the recovery-step agent flirts with liability. The time-blindness team (Cluster 3) walks into free, pre-installed OS competitors (Google/Apple time-to-leave) and a beloved incumbent (Llama Life) after the skeptic already downgraded the cluster to ~5-6 underserved. The communication-debt team (Cluster 5) fights every AI email startup plus platform API gatekeepers. The waiting-mode team (Cluster 6) builds on a mechanism the contradictions ledger says is unvalidated ('no research specifically examines waiting mode' — two competing causal stories). I chose the #1-ranked cluster (everyday score 10, five researchers converged) and — critically — I built on the exact sentence the adversarial skeptic wrote after tearing the cluster down: the open slice is 'spontaneous, in-the-moment freeze rescue with no self-initiation required.' T-Minus is that sentence turned into architecture: the trigger lives outside the user (inbound call), the rescue budget is one tap, and the launch sequence is a live negotiation no alarm, video, or list can perform. On Cluster 2, I don't promise better retention — I change what retention requires: every competitor needs the user to remember to open something, while T-Minus only needs them to answer a phone, and it detects and adapts when they stop (the Duolingo pattern the verdict confirmed no task tool has). It ships in 30 days with no app-store dependency — a phone number, a voice model, and a web page. And where every judge expects an ADHD app to quietly bill the forgetful, our subscription pauses itself. The other theses need the market to forgive their gaps. Mine was designed inside the skeptic's own verdict — attack it and you're attacking the research.

theses.one_liner: A rally co-driver for your day: an AI time-guardian that takes legal-custody-level responsibility for your appointments, learns your personal time-estimation error from observed reality, and hands the hours between events back to you.
theses.target_user: Maya, 34, a hybrid-remote product manager diagnosed with ADHD at 31 — the exact cohort where new diagnoses nearly doubled 2020-2022 (women 23-49, Epic Research). She has a calendar-driven job with 2-6 meetings a day, a household, and money to spend. Her specific pattern: an afternoon dentist appointment vaporizes her whole morning (waiting mode); she tells her husband a drive takes 5 minutes when it takes 20 (ADDitude reader Natalie's exact quote); and twice a week she surfaces from a work or gaming hyperfocus hole having missed dinner or a call. She has already bought and abandoned Tiimo, a Time Timer, and Todoist. She does not need another planner — she needs something that watches the clock so she doesn't have to. She is NOT the unmedicated, unemployed, or crisis-stage user; Pacenote assumes a smartphone, a digital calendar, and a job worth being on time for.
winning_problem: Waiting Mode: One Appointment Paralyzes the Whole Day (Cluster 6)
Time Blindness: Broken Duration Estimates, Chronic Lateness, Missed Appointments (Cluster 3)
theses.product_concept:
Pacenote is a phone app built on one metaphor: the rally co-driver. A rally driver takes blind corners at 100mph not because they can see the road, but because a trusted voice beside them is reading the pacenotes and has never once been wrong. Adults with ADHD have no internal pacenotes — the research's time family is one broken organ showing three symptoms: they cannot feel an appointment approaching (waiting mode), cannot feel duration (time blindness), and cannot feel elapsed time inside absorption (hyperfocus). Pacenote is the external organ. It connects to your existing calendar (no new system to build or maintain — this is the anti-abandonment bet), and for each 'anchor' event it performs an explicit CUSTODY HANDOFF: you tap 'Guardian engaged,' the event visually leaves your day, and a deterministic, unmissable escalation ladder — novel notification, full-screen takeover with fresh audio, and finally an actual telephone call that rings through silent mode — takes over the vigilance. The app shows you a running reliability receipt ('47 handoffs, 0 misses') because the skeptic-verified root cause of waiting mode is distrust of one's own alarms after past misses; trust is built with receipts, not promises.

A day with it: at 8:40am Maya gets a 40-second brief. Her 3pm dentist appointment isn't shown as '3pm' — the LLM has decomposed its true cost (find insurance card, dress, 22-minute drive on live traffic, plus HER historically observed 12-minute leave-late error) into a leave-by of 2:19, and the day renders as what she actually has: 'You have 3h50m of protected open road before prep starts. Guardian engaged. Go.' The morning that used to be dead waiting-mode time is explicitly released, and the calendar goes quiet — the event is hidden from ambient view until T-minus, attacking the second hypothesized waiting-mode mechanism (attentional dominance) alongside the first (trust). At 2:12 the ladder starts gently; if she's deep in something, it escalates to the phone ringing at 2:19. She has learned, from receipts, that she is allowed to think about literally anything else until that phone rings.

The same organ works on the way out of absorption. When Maya arms a focus session (or, on Android, Pacenote passively notices a 3-hour single-app hole), it doesn't just interrupt — it stages a context-preserving exit: a 15-second voice brain-dump ('park the thread') that the LLM structures into a re-entry card waiting for her later ('you were about to check whether the API retries on 429'). The skeptic confirmed no product on the market does either automatic focus-hole detection or thread-parking; the fear of losing the mental thread is why pausing feels unsafe. And underneath everything runs the calibration loop: Pacenote silently logs planned-vs-actual (geofenced departure times, session lengths, snooze behavior) and corrects future plans automatically — it never asks Maya to review a dashboard. Google Maps corrects for traffic; nothing corrects for Maya. That personal error model is the compounding asset: the app is more accurate in week 6 than week 1, which is the exact inversion of the novelty cliff that kills every other ADHD tool.
theses.core_loop: 1) MORNING BRIEF (40 sec, push or open): the day renders as a horizon bar — anchor events with LLM-computed true cost (prep steps + live travel + personal error buffer) and, more importantly, the green 'open road' blocks between them, sized honestly. 2) CUSTODY HANDOFF (2 taps): for each anchor, 'Engage guardian.' The event dims out of ambient view; the reliability receipt increments its 'watching' state. This is the ritual that converts 5 dead pre-appointment hours into usable time. 3) OPEN ROAD (passive): during green blocks the app is silent except an optional glanceable countdown widget ('2h10 safe'). Nothing to check, log, or groom. 4) T-MINUS LADDER (deterministic): prep-start nudge with novel LLM wording → full-screen takeover with a sound it has never used before → real phone call through silent mode at leave-by. Post-event: receipt increments ('48/48'). 5) FOCUS EXIT (when armed/detected): hourly time-anchors ('3 hours elapsed; it is getting dark') → at exit time, 'park the thread' 15-second voice capture → structured re-entry card appears when the anchor event ends. 6) SILENT CALIBRATION (no user action): geofence logs actual departure, session logs actual duration; the error model updates and tomorrow's leave-by shifts. Once a week, one sentence of proof: 'You said 5 minutes; your last 9 trips took 18-24. I have been padding accordingly.' The loop has zero daily obligations — it fires only when the calendar has an anchor, so a week of ignoring it leaves nothing overdue, broken, or red.
theses.why_ai_is_essential: Four load-bearing AI functions, each impossible pre-LLM: (1) TRUE-COST DECOMPOSITION — turning an arbitrary calendar string ('Dentist 3pm', 'Pick up Sam from soccer') into task-specific prep steps and durations requires open-world commonsense inference; rule-based apps make the user enter prep time manually, i.e., they trust the exact faculty that is broken (the ADDitude 5-vs-20-minute quote is a self-estimate failure). (2) ANTI-HABITUATION WORDING ENGINE — LLM-generated, never-repeating nudge copy in a chosen voice, driven by a bandit over channel/sound/timing/phrasing. Habituation to identical alarm stimuli is the documented death of every reminder system ('invisible within weeks, sometimes days'); infinite non-repeating variation was not manufacturable before generative models. (3) THREAD PARKING — converting a 15-second rambling voice dump mid-hyperfocus into a structured re-entry card is speech-to-structured-intent, pure LLM territory, and it is the feature the skeptic confirmed nobody has ('context-preserving exit... no found product does either'). (4) NARRATED CALIBRATION — a statistical error model only changes behavior if the user believes it; the LLM converts a distribution into one disarming, personal sentence. What breaks without AI: strip the LLM and Pacenote degrades into exactly Tiimo-plus-Twilio — another self-configured timer the user must estimate for, habituates to, and abandons; the entire differentiated surface (prep inference, novelty, thread capture, believable correction) is generative. The deterministic escalation ladder alone is 2015 technology; that's why it never worked as a product — it punished users with a screaming inflexible alarm for plans the user had mis-estimated in the first place.
non_ai_features: The escalation ladder itself is deterministic, hard-coded state machine logic — an LLM never decides WHETHER to fire a wake step or place the call. The product's entire value rests on '48/48 handoffs'; a stochastic model in the firing path would make the trust guarantee a lie. AI writes the words; a cron-grade scheduler pulls the trigger.
The reliability receipt is plain arithmetic (engaged anchors vs. on-time handoffs), locally computed and auditable in-app. Trust receipts must be boring.

The phone-call channel (Twilio) is dumb by design: it rings, plays a short recorded line, requires a keypress to acknowledge, and re-rings if unacknowledged. No conversation, no cleverness, no failure modes.
Geofenced departure logging and screen-session detection are raw deterministic sensing — the calibration model consumes their output, but the capture layer never interprets.

The day-horizon bar and countdown widget are static rendering of computed times, deliberately spartan — the visual timer category is saturated (Tiimo, Time Timer, TimeSee) and we refuse to compete on countdown UI.
The amnesty/pause button and billing auto-pause are rule-based: one tap suspends all guardianship and billing with no AI-judged friction, no exit interview, no win-back model.
theses.anti_habituation_design: Cluster 2 kills tools via four mechanisms; Pacenote has a concrete counter for each. (1) ALARM HABITUATION → three-layer defense: a Duolingo-style sleeping-bandit (the published KDD 2020 approach) selects across channel × sound × timing × wording and self-silences arms the user ignores; LLM copy never repeats verbatim; and the ladder terminates in a channel that physiologically cannot habituate silently — an actual ringing phone call requiring a keypress, which also cannot be reflex-swiped like a notification. Ignore-detection is explicit: if Maya swipes three prep nudges in a week, Pacenote says 'these aren't landing — switching you to calls-only for anchors' instead of shouting louder into the void. (2) NOVELTY CLIFF / SETUP COLLAPSE → there is nothing to set up or maintain: no task list, no projects, no tags. The only inventory is the calendar Maya already keeps for her job. Onboarding is: connect calendar, verify phone number, engage first anchor — under 3 minutes. Crucially, the value curve is inverted: the personal error model is fed by passive geofence/session data from day one, so the product is objectively better at week 6 than week 1 — the moment every other tool goes stale is the moment Pacenote's corrections start being eerily right, and the weekly one-sentence proof ('padding your estimates by 14 min — you've been on time 9 of 9') makes the compounding visible. (3) SHAME SPIRAL / BROKEN STREAK → structurally impossible: usage is event-driven, not streak-driven. There are no streaks, no overdue counters, no red badges. If Maya ignores Pacenote for three weeks, reopening shows exactly two things: her intact lifetime receipt ('31/31') and today's horizon. Lapsing leaves no debris, so re-onboarding requires no courage. (4) THE TOOL BECOMING A TASK → the daily obligation is 40 seconds of reading plus two taps, and even skipping that costs nothing — guardianship auto-engages for calendar events matching learned anchor patterns. The week-6 test, concretely: by week 6 Maya has ~15 receipts, a calibrated leave-late correction, and at least one story where the phone rang while she was genuinely absorbed and she made the appointment anyway. That story — 'I stopped guarding the clock and it caught me' — is the retention event, and it is also the mechanism the waiting-mode root cause says restores the lost hours.

competitors.name: Tiimo
competitors.gap: Apple's 2025 App of the Year, explicitly content-markets against waiting mode — but everything is a self-configured visual timer built on the user's own estimates. The skeptic's verdict names the hole exactly: 'all are self-set alarms/timers, which the root-cause analysis says users distrust... no product occupies the trusted external time-guardian wedge.' Tiimo makes time visible; it does not take custody of it.

competitors.name: BugMe
competitors.gap: 12-tier escalating screen-takeover alarm for breaking hyperfocus (launched July 2026) — proof of demand for unignorable escalation. But it is a single-moment alarm the user must remember to set, with no whole-day model, no waiting-mode custody ritual, no automatic focus-hole detection, no thread parking, and no learning loop. It's our ladder without our co-driver.

theses.business_model: $9/month or $72/year, 30-day full trial with NO card required (a card-first trial is itself an ADHD tax — Cluster 2 documents 'gamification novelty decays in 4-8 weeks while annual billing continues'). The anti-ADHD-tax architecture is a product feature and the marketing story: (1) BILLING AUTO-PAUSE — if no anchor has been engaged for 45 days, billing pauses itself and emails 'You're not using Pacenote, so you're not paying for it. Your receipts (31/31) are safe whenever you return.' This converts Cluster 2's abandonment cliff from silent revenue extraction into the single most screenshot-shareable trust move in the category. (2) One-tap in-app cancel, no exit survey, no retention flow. (3) No-questions refund on any renewal within 60 days. (4) Annual is offered, never pushed, and emails you 7 days before renewing. A product whose entire thesis is 'trust me with your appointments' cannot bill like a gym; monetizing forgetfulness would falsify the brand. Unit economics hold because the marginal cost is small: LLM calls are short (brief generation, prep inference, nudge copy) and Twilio calls cost ~$0.02 each with a realistic 1-3 calls/day ceiling — comfortably inside $9/mo gross margin. Wedge market: even 25k subscribers of the 15.5M diagnosed US adults (CDC) is a $2.7M ARR business for a 2-3 person team, in an ADHD-app market at ~$1.9B growing 12-17% CAGR with no dominant winner.
theses.month_one_scope: SHIPS IN 30 DAYS (2 engineers + 1 designer/founder, single platform first — Android, because passive session-sensing and full-screen takeover are unrestricted there): Google Calendar read sync; morning brief with LLM true-cost decomposition (prep steps + Google Maps travel + fixed default buffer); custody handoff ritual with quiet-calendar event dimming; the full deterministic escalation ladder including Twilio phone call with keypress-acknowledge and re-ring; reliability receipt; day-1 instrumentation of planned-vs-actual (geofenced departures, notification response latency, session lengths); billing auto-pause logic; amnesty button. That is a complete, honest product for waiting mode + lateness — the two highest-confidence clusters — and every piece is proven tech (calendar API, FCM, Twilio, one LLM prompt family). DELIBERATELY LATER: personal error-model corrections go live month 2 (they need 3-4 weeks of the data month 1 starts collecting — shipping 'calibration' before it has data would be theater); thread-parking voice capture month 2; passive hyperfocus-hole detection month 2 on Android, month 3 on iOS via user-armed focus sessions only (Screen Time API limits make passive iOS detection dishonest to promise); iOS app month 3; bedtime guardian and partner/household features quarter 2. The month-1 cut line is principled: ship the trust engine first, because receipts take calendar-time to accumulate and the error model takes data-time to converge — both clocks must start at launch.
riskiest_assumptions: THE MECHANISM BET: waiting mode has zero formal research (The Conversation, verbatim-confirmed) and the dataset flags two competing causal stories — distrust of one's own alarms vs. attentional dominance of the upcoming event. Pacenote hedges by attacking both (receipts + escalation for trust; custody ritual + event-dimming for salience), but if pre-event paralysis persists even when the alarm is guaranteed, the flagship 'hands your hours back' claim collapses to a nice leave-on-time app. Testable in week 1 of beta: do users self-report starting tasks in guarded pre-anchor windows?

THE INTRUSION TOLERANCE BET: the terminal channel is a real phone call. If users disable it after one embarrassing ring in a meeting, the ladder loses its non-habituable floor and the trust guarantee with it. Mitigation (context-aware suppression rules) is in tension with the guarantee itself.

THE ZERO-MISS BET: receipts assume near-perfect delivery. Dead battery, DND edge cases, or an FCM delay causing even one missed anchor damages trust super-linearly — the exact past-miss trauma that created the distrust we're trying to repair. Requires redundant channels (SMS + call + push) and an honest 'delivery confirmed' architecture from day one.

THE COLD-START-VS-CLIFF RACE: the compounding error model is the anti-abandonment story, but it needs 3-4 weeks of data — meaning the retention asset matures exactly when the novelty cliff hits. Month one must retain on receipts and relief alone.

THE FREE-ALTERNATIVE SQUEEZE: Google/Apple give away travel-time alerts; a skeptic will say the paid delta is 'a phone call and a story.' The bet is that custody + calibration + receipts is a categorically different product, not a premium notification — if users can't feel that difference in the trial month, willingness-to-pay dies.

THE PLATFORM BET: full-screen takeover, reliable scheduled escalation, and passive session detection are all constrained on iOS, where the target demographic disproportionately lives. Android-first is right for capability but may be wrong for the customer; the iOS version must fake nothing it can't guarantee.

theses.why_i_win: Every rival thesis builds where the skeptics said the field is already occupied or the month-one build is impossible. The initiation team must displace Dubbii (500k users) and Focusmate in a category the skeptic downgraded from 9 to ~5-6 underserved, with 'mixed' efficacy evidence. The life-admin/ADHD-tax team needs bank integrations, act-on-my-behalf trust, and phone-call automation that cannot responsibly ship in 30 days. The communication team fights Slack/Gmail platform gatekeeping plus Rewind-grade privacy objections. A meta-problem team has a design principle, not a product. Temporal holds the three highest-confidence surviving verdicts in the dataset — waiting mode and hyperfocus exit both at 0.75, the top scores the skeptics awarded — with the open wedges named in the skeptics' own words: 'no product occupies the trusted external time-guardian wedge,' 'automatic detection of a multi-hour focus session combined with context-preserving exit — no found product does either,' and the closed-loop personal estimate-error learner that Llama Life displays but doesn't act on. One product covers all three because they are one deficit: no internal time sense. The build is honest month-one tech (calendar API + notifications + Twilio + one LLM prompt family — no bank, no email scraping, no hardware). And the Cluster 2 meta-killer is answered structurally, not rhetorically: no streaks to break, no inventory to groom, an error model that makes week 6 better than week 1, and a receipt counter that converts reliability into the one currency ADHD users have never been given by their own tools — trust. Where every other thesis asks the user to do something, Pacenote's pitch is the opposite and therefore survives the user's worst days: stop watching the clock; I've got it.

theses.one_liner: Snap a photo of the scary envelope and Recoup reads it, tells you the real dollars at stake, and does 90% of the fixing — turning the ADHD tax into a running refund.
theses.target_user: Maya, 34, diagnosed at 31 — the exact surge cohort (new ADHD diagnoses among women 23-49 nearly doubled 2020-2022, per Epic Research). Employed marketing manager, ~$75k, has the money to pay her bills but has not opened the mail pile on the kitchen counter in six weeks. Three zombie subscriptions, a parking ticket she knows is doubling, a $140 return riding around in her trunk past the window, and a shame loop where every fee makes the next envelope harder to open. She has already tried Todoist, a paper planner, and Rocket Money. She does not need another reminder; she needs someone to open the envelope and deal with the contents.
winning_problem: Cluster 4: Life Admin Avoidance & the ADHD Tax (bills, mail, subscriptions, returns, fines)
Cluster 2 (as design constraint, not target): Every Coping Tool Stops Working — habituation + abandonment
theses.product_concept:
Recoup is an AI admin harm-reduction service built on one behavioral insight from the research: "open the envelope you have to deal with the contents. Don't open the envelope nothing to deal with" (TotallyADD forum). The avoidance is not of the paper — it is of the dealing. So Recoup decouples them. The user's only job is to point a camera at the pile (opened or unopened; envelope windows, return addresses, and franking marks carry signal) or forward a dreaded email to their Recoup address. The AI does the dealing: identifies what each item is, extracts the deadline and the dollars at stake, flags what is safely ignorable junk — telling an avoider "7 of these 11 items require nothing from you" is itself a product moment — and converts the rest into pre-executed actions.

A day with Recoup: at 9am, one notification, never more, says "One move today: your parking ticket doubles from $85 to $170 on Friday. Tap to see the pre-filled online payment — or the pre-written hardship/contest letter if you want to fight it." Maya taps, reviews the extracted details against the photo of the actual ticket (the source image is always shown side-by-side, because a hallucinated deadline would be fatal to trust), approves, done in 90 seconds. Her Tax Meter ticks: "$85 in doubling averted. $312 recovered since March." Nothing else is asked of her today.

The deliberately targeted slice is exactly what the skeptic verdict identified as the unserved remainder: physical mail triage, returns execution, fine deadlines, and the shame/avoidance loop. Rocket Money owns bank-visible subscriptions; Recoup owns the pile — the paper and inbox dread that no Plaid integration can see. For the hardest recovery steps, Recoup drafts the thing the user cannot make themselves produce: the payment-plan request ("I filed bankruptcy at age 23, in large part because I just couldn't call and work out payment plans" — ADDitude reader), the first-time late-fee waiver letter (issuers grant these routinely; nobody with ADHD-fueled shame asks), the cancellation email, the word-for-word phone script with the number pre-dialed. Recoup never moves money and never sends anything without a human tap.

The emotional design is amnesty-first. Items are never "overdue" in the UI; they re-rank by current dollars-at-stake ("$85 → $170 Friday"), because a consequence framed as money still to be saved invites action, while a red badge framed as failure triggers the documented shame-then-never-open-again spiral. Recoup is the accountant who says "here's what we can still recover," never the parent who asks why you waited.
theses.core_loop: 1) CAPTURE (10 seconds, whenever): user snaps photos of any mail/paper — no opening, sorting, or categorizing required — or forwards emails to their @recoup address. Capture is dumb-fast and offline-safe; AI processing happens after, never blocking the camera. 2) TRIAGE (AI, async): each item gets identity (who/what), deadline, dollars-at-stake, and an ignorability verdict; junk is dismissed with an explicit "requires nothing" stamp. 3) ONE MOVE A DAY (9am, single notification): Recoup surfaces exactly one action — the highest current dollars-at-stake item — pre-executed to ~90%: pre-filled payment page, drafted waiver letter, cancellation email, return QR code with the nearest drop-off, or a call script. 4) CONFIRM (90 seconds): user checks the extraction against the source photo shown alongside, taps approve/send. 5) METER: the Tax Meter increments with real dollars averted or recovered; the weekly summary is money, not streaks. Lapse branch: if nothing is snapped and notifications are ignored 3 days running, Recoup switches framing once, then self-silences: "I'll hold everything until you snap something." The pile waits without judgment; the next scary envelope re-triggers the loop from the outside.
theses.why_ai_is_essential: The load-bearing job is reading arbitrary documents and drafting bespoke recovery actions, and both were impossible pre-LLM. (1) Triage over unbounded document space: a parking authority notice, an HOA letter, a medical EOB, a jury summons, a final-notice utility bill, and a fake-urgent car-warranty mailer all look different, come from a long tail of millions of senders, and no integration-based product (Plaid, biller APIs) will ever cover them — which is precisely why Rocket Money stops at bank-visible subscriptions. Multimodal LLMs read a crumpled photographed letter and output sender, obligation, deadline, amount, and consequence in one pass. (2) Ignorability judgment: deciding "this requires nothing from you" is a semantic classification with real stakes; rules and OCR templates cannot do it, and it is half the emotional value. (3) Recovery drafting: the fee-waiver letter, the payment-plan email, the contest-the-fine appeal, the retention-flow-resistant cancellation message — each must be composed against the specific creditor, amount, and user situation. This is the step the skeptic confirmed the whole market leaves to the user, and it is exactly the step the bankruptcy-at-23 quote shows people cannot self-initiate. Without AI, Recoup degrades into either a scanning app (capture with no dealing) or a human-VA service (unit economics of $30+/hr). With AI, the marginal cost of "dealing" approaches zero, which is what makes a $9/month price on a money-recovery service possible at all.
non_ai_features: Deadline math and the fine-doubling countdown: once a date and amount are human-confirmed, all countdowns, escalation projections ($85 → $170 Friday), and the 9am scheduler are deterministic code. Dates that cost money must never pass through a generative step twice.
The Tax Meter: a plain arithmetic ledger of dollars averted/recovered. It must be exactly and boringly correct, because it is the trust anchor and the retention hook.

Capture flow: camera, photo queue, offline storage, email forward-in. Zero AI at capture time — the snap must never lag, fail, or wait on a model, because capture is the one behavior we ask the user to sustain.
The one-notification-per-day cap, quiet hours, and the 3-ignores-then-silence rule: hard-coded policy, not model discretion. An LLM deciding when to nag is how you habituate users out of the product.

Human-in-the-loop send/pay gates: nothing is ever mailed, emailed, or paid without an explicit tap, and Recoup never holds payment credentials or moves money. This is a trust and safety line, kept deliberately dumb.

Side-by-side source verification UI: every extracted date/amount is displayed next to the original photo region it came from, so the human confirms against ground truth rather than trusting the model.
theses.anti_habituation_design: Cluster 2's mechanics are answered point by point. (1) Structural advantage first: Recoup is externally triggered and episodic, not internally motivated and daily. Habit trackers die because the product must generate the trigger and the reward is symbolic; here the trigger is the physical mail that keeps arriving regardless of app engagement, and the reward is variable-magnitude real money — the one reward class that does not habituate, because it is not a token. A lapsed user is re-engaged by the world (a scary envelope) rather than by a notification they have gone blind to. (2) No streaks, no overdue: items cannot become "overdue" in the UI — they re-rank by current dollars-at-stake, so the 87-red-tasks shame wall (thawly.ai's documented Todoist failure) is structurally impossible. There is nothing to break, so nothing breaks the user. (3) Pile amnesty on re-entry: opening the app after 5 silent weeks shows exactly one screen — "Welcome back. One move today, worth $170" — never a backlog. Re-onboarding is shame-free by construction, answering the JMIR abandonment cliff (median 70% within 100 days, n=525,824) with a product where returning at day 101 works as well as day 2. (4) Adaptive notifications that concede: one per day max; after 3 ignores the framing changes once (deadline-consequence vs money-recovered vs "want me to just hold everything?"), then Recoup self-silences Duolingo-style ("These aren't landing — I'll wait for your next snap") rather than training reflex-swiping. The skeptic showed Duolingo proved this works (KDD 2020 bandit paper); no admin tool has copied it. (5) Week-6 concrete story: onboarding targets a first real dollar win inside week 1 (a fine caught before doubling, a waiver letter granted, a zombie trial killed — median findable value in a six-week mail pile is nonzero by definition of the cluster). By week 6, Maya's Tax Meter reads a real number like $200-400. Abandoning a habit app costs nothing; going dark on Recoup means the next $170 doubling hits unwatched — loss aversion on real money is the retention mechanism, and it strengthens rather than decays with accumulated evidence that the meter is honest. (6) If she still lapses, the auto-pause billing clause (below) means the product harmlessly hibernates instead of becoming a resented zombie charge — which is what makes her comfortable coming back.

theses.business_model: Flat $9/month (or $10 with the concierge letter-sending tier later), deliberately NOT a percentage of savings — Rocket Money's 30-60% first-year-savings skim extracts the most from the people recovering the most, which is a predator's version of alignment. Three structural anti-ADHD-tax commitments, marketed loudly because they are the brand: (1) Auto-pause billing: if you do not open Recoup for a full billing month, your subscription pauses automatically and you are not charged — the product contractually cannot become the zombie subscription it exists to kill. This is the signature trust move and, per Cluster 2's subscription-forgetfulness evidence, the strongest possible differentiator in a market that monetizes ADHD lapses. (2) One-tap cancellation in-app, zero retention flow, effective immediately with pro-rata refund on annual. (3) No auto-converting free trial; instead a free tier capped at 5 items/month that stays free forever, so trial-forgetting can never bill anyone. Unit economics: vision-LLM triage plus drafting costs cents per item at 2026 prices; a user averting one $35 late fee or one $170 fine doubling per quarter is visibly net-positive against $27/quarter, and the Tax Meter makes that ROI legible inside the product — the subscription justifies itself with a number, monthly. Break-even honesty is the retention pitch: "If Recoup hasn't saved you more than it costs, the meter will say so, and cancelling takes one tap."
theses.month_one_scope: SHIPS IN 30 DAYS (2-3 engineers, iOS-first app + thin backend): camera capture with photo queue; email forward-in address; multimodal LLM triage (sender, type, deadline, amount, consequence, ignorability) with confidence gating; side-by-side human confirmation UI for every date/amount; deterministic deadline engine and fine-escalation countdowns; One-Move-a-Day scheduler with the notification cap and 3-ignores-self-silence rule; recovery drafts for the top 5 action types (late-fee waiver letter, payment-plan request, subscription cancellation email, fine payment walkthrough/contest letter, return checklist with carrier drop-off lookup); Tax Meter ledger; pile-amnesty re-entry screen; auto-pause billing via standard subscription APIs. All of this is app + LLM + phone camera — no hardware, no bank credentials, no FDA anything. LATER (months 2-6): optional Plaid read-only for zombie-subscription detection (only after trust exists — bank linking on day 1 is an avoider's abandonment point); voice-AI phone calls to creditors with user listening in; automated return-label generation and pickup scheduling; USPS Informed Delivery ingestion so mail is triaged before it is even opened; shared-household mode for the partner dynamic in the research; UK localization. EXPLICITLY NEVER: moving money, holding payment credentials, medication features, credit-repair claims.
riskiest_assumptions: The capture step survives avoidance: the thesis bets that photographing a closed envelope is emotionally cheap enough to do while opening it is not. If the wall of awful extends to pointing a camera at the pile, the loop never starts. This is the 'fix requires the failing faculty' trap applied to us, and it is testable in week 1 with 20 users and a mail pile.

Extraction accuracy is trust-critical and asymmetric: one hallucinated deadline that costs a user a doubled fine ends the relationship (and the word-of-mouth). The human-confirm UI mitigates but also adds friction; the bet is that confirming against a shown photo is low enough friction to survive.

Recovery drafts convert to real dollars often enough to feed the Tax Meter: fee-waiver grant rates, payment-plan acceptance, and contest-letter success are assumed but unmeasured for this population; if the meter stays near $0 for a median user's first month, the retention story collapses.

Flat-fee willingness to pay against 'free-feeling' competitors: Rocket Money's skim is invisible, $9/month is visible. The bet is that the ADHD community's documented rage at predatory billing converts into preference for honest pricing, not just approval of it.

Episodic engagement is compatible with subscription economics: auto-pause billing means lapsed users generate $0 instead of zombie revenue — ethically core, financially untested. Modeled LTV depends on reactivation by scary envelopes, which is plausible but unproven.

Privacy comfort: users must photograph financial and legal documents into an AI service. The research shows they already leave these documents rotting in public view on counters, suggesting low sensitivity-in-practice, but stated privacy preferences may differ.

The Monzo 49%/£1,600 figures are bank-commissioned self-report; the sizing bet really rests on the objective Science Advances registry data (6x default risk by 40). If the everyday recoverable-dollar frequency is lower than the survey implies, week-1 wins get scarcer.

theses.why_i_win: Three arguments, in ascending order of force. (1) Best-verified ground: Cluster 4 carries the strongest skeptic verdict in the dataset (0.8 — versus 0.6 for initiation paralysis and habituation, 0.62 for time blindness) and the highest AI-leverage score (10). Uniquely, its evidence includes objective national-registry outcomes (Science Advances: 6x credit default at 40), not just self-report and TikTok virality. Teams building on initiation must displace Dubbii's 500k users in a crowded body-doubling field; time-blindness teams must beat free OS-level travel alerts; waiting-mode teams build on a phenomenon with literally zero formal research and an unvalidated mechanism. I build on the cluster the adversarial process attacked hardest and dented least — and my product occupies exactly the remainder the skeptic certified as unserved: mail triage, returns, fines, and the shame loop. (2) Only cluster with a self-funding retention story: every rival product must fight the 70%-abandonment cliff armed with symbolic rewards (streaks, calm, 'progress'), which is precisely what habituates. (3) The business model is the moat: this category's incumbents monetize ADHD (savings skims, hard-to-cancel subscriptions, FTC sanctions). A product whose billing auto-pauses when unused is not just ethical garnish — it is the single most credible thing you can say to this audience, it is cheap for me and ruinous for skim-dependent incumbents to copy, and it converts the community's loudest grievance into distribution. Judges should ask every team two questions: 'what does your user have to show for week 6?' and 'what happens when your user forgets you exist?' I am the only thesis whose answers are 'a dollar amount' and 'the bill stops.'

theses.one_liner: Molt is a five-anchor daily companion for ADHD adults that detects the moment you start tuning it out and sheds its own skin — new voice, new mechanics, new nudges — before your brain files it under 'ignore.'
theses.target_user: Maya, 34, diagnosed with ADHD at 31 — one of the post-2020 surge cohort of women 23-49 whose new-diagnosis rate nearly doubled from 2020 to 2022 (Epic Research). She has a full-time job, a partner, a household, and a planner graveyard: Todoist (abandoned with 87 overdue tasks), Notion (collapsed after the weekend she spent building it), Finch (the bird is fine, she just stopped opening it), two paper planners, and Structured. She does not need another task system; she needs five recurring things to actually fire every day — take meds, leave on time, start the laundry chain, deal with the mail pile, go to bed — and every tool that ever handled them went invisible within three weeks. She is the natural first customer named in the market research (Cluster 12) and the persona behind the 'hundreds of $$ on planners' App Store review.

Medication Management (the reminder-habituation slice only: reminder apps habituate and get abandoned)

theses.product_concept:
Molt is not a task manager. It is a reminder organism that holds a hard-capped set of five recurring daily anchors — the meds dose, the leave-time, the laundry chain, the mail pile, the wind-down — and delivers them through nudges that are never the same twice. Every nudge is generated fresh by an LLM: different wording, different tone, different persona, different modality (text, voice note, lock-screen line, a question instead of a command). Underneath sits the real product: a habituation-detection engine. Every nudge is an instrument — Molt measures response latency, dismissal-versus-action ratio, and open-rate drift per anchor and per channel. When your response curve to a channel starts decaying, that is treated as a fire alarm, not a churn statistic: the engine mutates harder, rotates modality, or honestly retires the channel ('You've swiped the 8am ping 4 days straight. I'm going to stop pinging and try something else.'). This is Duolingo's published sleeping-bandit notification architecture (KDD 2020) — the one mainstream system proven to detect and adapt to being ignored — extended from streak reminders over a finite template bank to open-ended life logistics over a generative model, which the skeptic verdict itself confirms no to-do or reminder app currently does.

We chose the reminder/routine surface deliberately, because it proves the engine best: alarm blindness is the fastest, most legible habituation failure in the whole dataset ('invisible within weeks, sometimes days'), and reminders give the cleanest per-event telemetry — every nudge either got a response or it didn't, with a timestamp. Tasks and calendars are noisy surfaces; a nudge is a single-trial habituation experiment, dozens of times a week, per user. Molt is a machine for running those experiments and acting on them.

A day with Molt: at 7:40 a morning card arrives — today it's a three-word checklist; yesterday it was a 12-second voice note from 'Marrow,' this fortnight's persona; you one-tap confirm today's anchors in under a minute. Through the day, anchors fire as one-tap done / not-now / stop-this nudges. Anything you don't do silently expires at midnight — no red badge, no overdue counter, no streak to break, ever. On Sunday, Molt visibly molts: new skin, a persona hand-off, one mechanic retired, one new mechanic introduced, 90-second re-onboard. If you vanish for a week — and you will, we plan for it — Molt greets you with a single question ('Same five anchors, or has life moved?'), never a backlog. If you vanish for 30 days, your billing auto-pauses and Molt hibernates. The product's whole personality is built around one bet: for this user, the abandonment curve is a design outcome, not destiny — which is exactly what the research's own contradiction #6 concluded (simple, guilt-free, no-maintenance apps retain ADHD users far better).
theses.core_loop: 1) MORNING CARD (≤60 sec): a generated brief arrives in a fresh form each day (checklist / voice note / single question / lock-screen line); user one-tap confirms or edits today's 3-5 anchors. 2) ANCHOR NUDGES: each anchor fires at its window as a freshly generated nudge — never-repeated wording, rotating tone/persona/modality — with exactly three responses: Done / Not now / Stop this. 'Not now' can take a free-text or voice reason; the LLM reschedules or reframes on the spot. 3) TELEMETRY TICK: every response or ignore updates that anchor's habituation curve (response latency drift, dismiss:action ratio). Decay past threshold triggers escalation-by-variation (modality swap, persona interjection) — never escalation-by-volume. Three straight ignores on a channel and it self-retires, out loud. 4) MIDNIGHT AMNESTY: undone anchors expire silently; no carryover, no red, no streaks anywhere in the product. 5) SUNDAY MOLT (90 sec): visible shed — new skin, persona hand-off with continuity ('Marrow briefed me on you'), one mechanic retired, one introduced, drawn from a rotation deck and biased by that user's telemetry. 6) LAPSE RE-ENTRY: absence >72h gets a one-question shame-free restart; absence >30 days pauses billing and sends one plain re-entry note.
theses.why_ai_is_essential: Non-repetition at the atomic level is the load-bearing mechanic, and it is economically impossible without generation. Duolingo's adaptive system — the proof this approach works — runs a bandit over a finite, human-written template bank and still converges on repetition; it took a dedicated team and works for exactly one domain (streak reminders). A two-person team cannot hand-write an inexhaustible, context-aware nudge library across five life domains, four personas, and multiple modalities; pre-LLM, 'novelty as a product primitive' meant a content treadmill no startup could afford, which is why nobody built this before. The LLM does four jobs no template system can: (1) generates every nudge fresh, conditioned on anchor, time, persona, recent history, and an explicit 'never resemble the last 30 nudges for this anchor' constraint; (2) converses at the moment of friction — when the user answers 'not now, my kid is sick,' it reschedules and reframes rather than re-firing; (3) writes each week's molt (persona hand-off letters, re-onboarding copy) so change feels authored, not random; (4) performs shame-free re-entry, summarizing nothing and asking one good question. Remove the AI and Molt collapses into exactly the static reminder app the research says goes invisible in days. What deliberately does NOT use AI is just as important — see the non-AI list: all safety, forgiveness, and scheduling guarantees are deterministic code, because a user rebuilding trust in reminders cannot be asked to trust a model's whims about WHETHER a nudge fires, only about HOW it reads.
non_ai_features: Anchor scheduling and notification delivery: plain deterministic timers/cron on-device — the guarantee that a nudge FIRES is never delegated to a model, only its content is; a hallucinated skip would destroy the exact trust the product exists to build

Midnight TTL expiry and the no-streak, no-overdue-counter, no-red-badge invariant: hard-coded product law, not model behavior — forgiveness must be unconditional and predictable, never 'decided' by AI

The five-anchor hard cap: a fixed constraint that keeps Molt from becoming a system to maintain (the Notion/Todoist two-week setup-collapse failure); the model is never allowed to suggest adding more structure
One-tap Done / Not now / Stop this response surface: fixed UI, zero generation, so the cost of responding stays near zero even when the nudge itself is novel
Habituation telemetry capture (latency, dismiss:action ratios, decay thresholds): deterministic statistics computed locally; the model consumes these signals but never computes them
Billing auto-pause after 30 days of inactivity and one-tap in-app cancellation: hard-coded, auditable, marketed as a guarantee

Travel/leave-time alerts defer to Google/Apple 'time to leave' rather than rebuilding them — per the skeptic's Cluster 3 verdict, free OS features already solve traffic-corrected departure; Molt only makes the leave-anchor salient
theses.anti_habituation_design: Eight concrete mechanics, in two layers. DETECTION LAYER (respond to decay): (1) Per-anchor, per-channel habituation curves — response latency drift and dismiss:action ratio computed on every nudge event; a statistically rising ignore-rate is the product's primary alarm. (2) Escalation-by-variation, never volume: decay triggers modality rotation (text→voice→lock-screen→widget) and persona interjection, because repetition-louder is the documented failure mode of alarms. (3) Honest self-silencing: a channel ignored 3 consecutive times retires itself and says so — the Duolingo-validated move ('these reminders don't seem to be working') that paradoxically re-earns attention. PREEMPTION LAYER (change before decay, because ADHD habituation speed is unverified — the 'days not weeks' claim is vendor-sourced, so we refuse to rely on detection alone): (4) Atomic non-repetition — no nudge for an anchor may resemble its last 30 predecessors; novelty at the message level is the default state, not a response. (5) The Sunday Molt — scheduled, visible self-change (skin, persona hand-off, one mechanic retired, one introduced) on a cadence faster than the 2-week novelty cliff and far inside the JMIR 100-day window; the app re-onboards itself in 90 seconds weekly, converting 're-onboarding' from a churn event into a ritual. (6) Midnight amnesty + no streaks: the two documented shame-abandonment triggers (87 overdue tasks; one broken streak) are structurally impossible — there is nothing in the interface that can accumulate against you. (7) Lapse-planned re-entry: >72h absence yields a one-question restart with zero backlog; the product treats abandonment as a scheduled state, not a failure, including 30-day hibernation with billing pause. (8) Week-6 responders as the only north-star metric: we instrument the JMIR cliff directly — percentage of week-1 actives still responding (not just opening) at day 42 — and every molt-deck mechanic lives or dies by its effect on that number. The 70% cliff is survived not by one trick but by making decay-detection the core competence: when mechanic X stops working for Maya, Molt is the only product in this market whose job description is noticing that and swapping X out.

competitors.name: Duolingo notification system (sleeping bandits, KDD 2020)
competitors.gap: The proof-of-concept and the ceiling of prior art: detects ignored reminders, self-silences, forgives streaks — but it is welded to one language-learning loop, draws from a finite human-written template bank, and its adaptation exists to protect Duolingo's engagement, not the user's life logistics. Nobody has ported the mechanism to daily-life anchors; the skeptic verdict explicitly found no to-do/reminder app doing Duolingo-style adaptation.

competitors.name: Finch
competitors.gap: Solves shame (non-punitive streaks, beloved by ADHD users) but not habituation: the pet loop is mechanically identical every day, content is a finite library, and there is no ignore-detection — forgiveness without variation. When the bird stops being novel there is no engine underneath to notice or respond.

competitors.name: Lunatask
competitors.gap: Markets against the exact install-abandon-forget cycle (their copy is in the research) but ships a static ADHD to-do app — the anti-abandonment claim is positioning, not mechanics; no telemetry-driven adaptation, no self-change, no generative nudges.

competitors.name: Routinery / Tiimo
competitors.gap: Visual routine sequencers are the epitome of what habituates: fixed sequences, identical prompts daily, streak mechanics. They are the category Molt's engine is built to outlive, and they have no answer to week 6 beyond aesthetics.

competitors.name: Alarmy
competitors.gap: Attacks reflex-swiping with friction (missions to dismiss) rather than novelty — friction defeats habituation briefly but breeds resentment and uninstall, and it cannot vary itself; it fights the swipe, not the tune-out.

competitors.name: Dubbii
competitors.gap: Owns initiation (Cluster 1) via follow-along body-doubling videos — a different problem — and its finite pre-recorded content library is itself exposed to the novelty cliff with no adaptive engine; not a competitor on habituation, and its 500k users are evidence this audience pays for companionship-shaped tools.

theses.business_model: $7.99/month or $59/year, one tier, with three hard-coded anti-ADHD-tax guarantees marketed as loudly as the product itself: (1) Billing auto-pause — 30 days of zero activity pauses your subscription automatically and emails you plainly; we structurally cannot earn zombie-subscription revenue, which is the documented trap ('gamification novelty decays in 4-8 weeks while annual billing continues'). This inverts the industry's incentive: because lapsed users stop paying, our revenue is mechanically coupled to our anti-habituation engine actually working — we get paid only while the product stays alive in someone's day, so the week-6 metric IS the revenue metric. (2) One-tap in-app cancellation, no retention flow, no email-to-cancel. (3) No auto-converting free trial: 21 days free (past the 2-week cliff on purpose — we want to be judged at week 3, not day 3), converting to paid only on an explicit yes; silence means it lapses to free-read-only. Recurring pricing is honest here rather than extractive because the marginal cost is real and ongoing — every nudge is a fresh LLM generation (~small-model pennies/user/day) and the molt deck is continuously authored. Annual buyers get a pro-rated pause credit under guarantee (1). Target: the 15.5M diagnosed US adults, entering via the late-diagnosed-women surge cohort, in a ~$1.9B ADHD-app market (2025) growing double digits with no dominant winner.
theses.month_one_scope: SHIPS IN 30 DAYS (2-3 people, iOS first since notification control is the product): five-anchor setup with hard cap; deterministic local scheduling; LLM nudge generation via API with 4 authored personas and a 30-nudge non-resemblance window; Done/Not-now/Stop-this response surface with free-text 'not now' rescheduling; telemetry capture (latency, dismiss:action) with a simple decay threshold; escalation-by-variation v0 (modality rotation across text/voice/lock-screen line) and 3-strike channel self-retirement; midnight TTL expiry, no-streak invariant; Sunday Molt v0 (skin + persona hand-off + copy, from a hand-built 8-week deck); 72h re-entry flow; Stripe billing with auto-pause and one-tap cancel. Explicitly NOT in month one: Android (month 2-3); adaptive bandit tuning of nudge arms (start with rules + thresholds, add the bandit once we have event volume); calendar/email integrations; voice conversations; any expansion past 5 anchors; community molt-pack marketplace; clinical claims of any kind. The month-one build is deliberately a thin organism around a fat measurement loop — the 8-week molt deck plus telemetry is the experiment apparatus for finding which mutations move day-42 responder retention.
riskiest_assumptions: Content-level novelty actually delays notification habituation: users may habituate to the CHANNEL (the buzz, the app icon) regardless of how fresh the words are — reflex-swiping happens before conscious registration, i.e., before wording can matter. Mitigation is baked in (modality rotation, self-retirement, lock-screen surface changes), but this is the thesis-level bet; if week-3 telemetry shows latency decay identical across novel vs. repeated nudges, the engine premise needs rework. The supporting 'ADHD habituates in days' claim is vendor-SEO-sourced (AFFiNE) with no peer-reviewed backing — we treat it as hypothesis, not fact.

The five-anchor cap holds: users burned by todo apps may still demand full task management, and a hard cap could read as 'toy' next to Todoist rather than as discipline. If churn interviews say 'too small,' the wedge is wrong even if the engine works.

Scheduled self-change delights rather than alienates: forced weekly persona/skin change could erode trust ('my tool is being random at me'), and the sizable AuDHD segment often actively wants sameness. The molt must feel authored and continuous (hand-off letters, preserved anchors) — if opt-outs of the molt exceed adoption, the marquee mechanic becomes a settings toggle.

Habituation telemetry is statistically usable at n=1: response-latency drift on ~5 nudges/day is a noisy signal; distinguishing 'tuning out' from 'busy week' within days, per user, may need more events than the surface generates. Fallback is leaning harder on the preemption layer (scheduled molts), which is unproven as retention math.

Unit economics of per-nudge generation plus a 21-day free trial plus billing auto-pause: three deliberately revenue-hostile choices stack; if week-6 responder retention lands under ~25-30%, auto-pause turns the base into confetti and LTV never covers CAC in a market where paid acquisition is bid up by VC-funded ADHD apps.

Day-42 responder retention can beat the field enough to matter: the JMIR 70%/100-day figure is a general-population floor, not an ADHD-specific benchmark, so our headline comparison lacks a true control; we must generate our own baseline cohort (static-nudge variant) in beta to prove the engine causes retention, or the primary claim is unfalsifiable.
